STUDY HALL COURSES:
Reporting On Politics 101
Reporting on local and national politics can feel opaque to those who have yet to crack the code. Perhaps more than even culture writing, politics requires knowledge of a specific, technical kind of language. In this
class
, Grace Byron will guide you on how to generate ideas, find outlets, and use the lingo that veteran politics reporters and editors use when building a story. From interviewing subjects, write-arounds, and opinion pieces, you will analyze a few pitches and stories to get a better sense of how to get started. You'll leave this one-hour class feeling prepared to start your political reporting journey and hopefully have a few ideas of how to get tips and pitch new editors.
Grace’s work has appeared in
The New Yorker,
Vogue
, and
The Nation
.
The 1.5 hour course will take place September 28th 10 AM PDT.

A Beginner’s Guide to Covering the Sex Industry
Sex work seems to be everywhere these days. Storylines about sex workers have popped up in shows like
Euphoria
,
Margo’s Got Money Troubles
, and
Hacks
. Yet even as OnlyFans has become a household name, few journalists actually understand the inner workings of this often underground industry — or how to build trust that’s needed to get sex worker sources to open up about these stories.
In this
course
, Lux Alptraum, an adult industry expert and one-time editor of the porn blog Fleshbot, will walk you through the basics of reporting on the sex industry. In addition to providing an overview of the different corners of the sex industry, she’ll also explain why so many sex workers do not trust journalists, and walk participants through the best practices for covering adult industry-related topics.
The 1.5 hour course will take place September 18th at 10 AM PDT/ 1 PM ET.

Don’t Make My Mistakes: A Guide to Reporting in Unfamiliar Places
by Hannah Docter-Loeb
Share on
Bluesky
I thought I had found the perfect story. While Googling around one day, I discovered a group of architects and engineers in a southern European city working to reduce urban heat by reprogramming ancient infrastructure, such as centuries-old aqueducts. Little had been written recently about the effort. As a science journalist based in the Netherlands, I was immediately intrigued. I was already going to the country for vacation, so I thought, “Why not try and write about it?”
I called a source involved in the project to get a sense of the story. He was a colorful character, full of good quotes and eager to show me the group’s work in person. I pitched an editor I had worked with previously, who greenlit the piece. Check, check, and check.
But when I arrived at my destination a few weeks later, I realized there was less “there” than I had thought. While touring the city’s cobblestone streets with the people working on the initiative, I learned that there was not much progress for me to report on. There also appeared to be some sort of dispute between different government bodies, uncertainty about who actually had jurisdiction over the infrastructure,
which was hampering the project. Aware that readers don’t want 1,000 words about bureaucracy in southern Europe and unsure how to pivot, I felt out of my depth. I emailed my editor voicing my concerns and asked to kill the story. I know it was the right choice, but this experience has haunted me since.
Scores of journalists report on countries or areas where they are not a native and do so successfully. What do the pros say about researching and reporting stories focused on a new community? I spoke to four journalists, some of whom have explored international reporting in sensitive areas.
Pick the right stories
Journalists who spoke to
Study Hall
said it’s easier to report on a new community when the focus of the story is an area where they have expertise. Jill Filipovic, a former lawyer and freelance journalist now based in Kenya, writes stories at the intersection of women’s rights, human rights, and reproductive rights. She authored a piece in 2021 for
The New York Review of Books
about how
safe abortion is not usually an option
in conflict and post-conflict zones, even though US international development aid was theoretically available to fund abortion in those places. To understand why, she secured grant funding and travelled to different countries, including Colombia and Uganda, where she spoke to
refugee women, sexual violence survivors, therapists, health workers, researchers, and country experts.
“I [wanted] to pull back a bit and tell a bigger global story instead of the definitive single story about one place,” she explained.
In her view, journalists who are not native to a community can add a fresh perspective to reporting on that community.
“You also need outsiders who are seeing these situations with fresh eyes and … [are] able to identify what is different about this place,” she said. Marlowe Starling, a freelance environmental journalist based in New York City, also said that being an outsider can be advantageous. For a feature story published by
Mongabay
in 2025, Starling
travelled to Panama
to report on conflicts between humans and jaguars
—
instances where the big cats attack livestock, and humans kill jaguars in retaliation. As a non-fluent Spanish speaker, she reported the story with the help of an interpreter.
According to Starling, writing the story for a Western audience helped add needed context around wildlife killings.
Western media generally portrays killing animals as bad, and the people who kill animals as immoral, but her reporting added nuance to that story, she said. People may kill wildlife to “
to make money (i.e. survive), to protect themselves, their families, or because of cultural reasons,” she added.
Prepare, prepare, prepare
Reporting on a new community, in a foreign country or domestically, requires more research than a typical reporting assignment, Alexander Sammon, a features reporter at
Slate
, told
Study Hall.
To prepare for a story he wrote for
Harper’s Magazine
about violent, local resistance to avocado growing in south-central Mexico, Sammon did a deep dive into the history of the conflict and the various players. Once he got a lay of the land, he called potential sources on the phone to discuss his story and find out what they would feel comfortable showing him.
His main piece of advice is to spend ample time in the community.  Sammon said there have been times when he ran into roadblocks while reporting remotely from New York City, such as struggling to get sources to speak to him. But once he arrived at his reporting destination, “the story really opened up.”
When he arrives at his destination, Sammon said he tries to squeeze in as much reporting time as possible. “
Once I’m at the place where I’m doing the story, I’m like, ‘alright, I'm just not going to take any time off, and I'm going to spend as many hours as I possibly can talking to people and just really listening,’” he said.
Starling suggests reading general information about the place, not just about the specific reporting topic. To report on solar power initiatives in Puerto Rico, for example, Starling began her research with topics like the island’s history as a US territory and how residents get their news.
She also emphasized the importance of discussing expectations
with translators and sources. On her reporting trip to Panama, there was a misunderstanding with some of the sources who thought that the news outlet was paying for everyone's accommodations, including the s
ources who did not live locally. Although it made for an awkward conversation, she clarified that outlets generally don’t pay for sources' expenses on a trip.
Collaborate
Outreach to local organizations can also help a journalist prepare for a travel assignment, sources told
Study Hall.
Emanuela Zuccalà, an Italian freelance journalist who has reported from countries in Europe, Africa, and the Middle East, will reach out to nonprofit organizations to ask for their support in arranging interviews. She’s careful to let the organizations know she is not doing advocacy for them.
For example, when reporting on female genital mutilation in Somaliland, Kenya, and Ethiopia, she connected with a nonprofit that promotes female empowerment in remote villages in Africa. The nonprofit helped her set up interviews and gave Zuccalà access to translators who already had connections to the communities she wanted to interview.
“If I go by myself, I'm a stranger, so they won't speak to me,” she said.
Filipovic regularly uses
fixers
–– someone hired to handle logistics and guide a foreign correspondent –– and often interviews journalists who report on the issue locally. “Local journalists are often such a wealth of information,” she said. If the journalist is doing a substantial amount of reporting, then she will ensure the reporter is included on the
byline
of the story.
Be patient and diligent
When entering a new community, Zuccalà emphasized the need to be patient when building source relationships. “[In the western world], we live in a
society where everything is very fast,” she said, but reporting on foreign communities, especially those that have experienced trauma, requires gentleness. “You have to start with very soft questions, [with] a conversation — and see when you can ask the [harder] question[s],” she said. She gave the example of when she interviewed women in Nigeria who had been kidnapped and raped by a terrorist group. “Sometimes it takes two hours just to [secure] two minutes of a video interview.”
Starling also emphasized researching cultural norms and being sure to respect them when you’re conducting an interview. For example, while on a reporting trip in Morocco, she learned it’s important to eat whatever food people bring you.
Making mistakes
With travel reporting, there are a lot of opportunities for something to go wrong. I made mistakes with my story about repurposed infrastructure by not doing enough research into the initiative ahead of time. It’s a mistake I won’t make again, but I’m wiser for it.
Starling said that reporting snafus are par for the course, and not to expect things to go smoothly. “Sometimes the story that you think you're going to end up reporting is not the story that is there; and if that happens, just roll with it.”
Interview with Molly Lambert
On the latest podcast
episode
